The NASA goals call for 33% reductions in block fuel burn and takeoff field length, and a 60% reduction in oxides of nitrogen (NOx) emissions, relative to the Boeing 737-800/CFM56-7B performance levels.

The independent design variables include sea level static thrust, wing reference area, fan pressure ratio, overall pressure ratio, fan drive system architecture, bypass nozzle architecture, and high- and low-pressure compressor work split.
The propulsion system is modeled as a boosted, two-spool, separate-flow turbofan, with performance analyzed using the NPSS code and aeromechanical design analyzed using the WATE code.
The advanced aircraft model is based on an analytical evolution of the Boeing 737-800, with a design cruise Mach number of 0.80, increased range, and increased use of composite materials.

Detailed takeoff and approach trajectory calculations are made for each aircraft-engine combination using FLOPS to capture the influence of airplane trajectory and engine throttling on noise certification levels.
NOx emissions are estimated based on the high-temperature regions inside the engine combustor, where nitrogen from the air oxidizes into nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2).
The optimization provides insight into the engine design options necessary to achieve multiple performance goals simultaneously, to help guide NASA's technology development efforts.
The analysis assumes engine and airframe technologies appropriate for a 2015-2020 service entry date, and builds on previous NASA system concept studies from 2008-2009.
Achieving the NASA goals for fuel burn, noise, emissions, and takeoff field length simultaneously is challenging due to the aggressive and often conflicting nature of these objectives.
The optimized solutions are expected to provide a broader set of design options compared to the previous NASA studies, by including fuel burn, noise, and emissions as optimization objectives.
The study uses a multi-objective optimization approach to explore the trade-offs between the various performance metrics for the advanced, single-aisle transport aircraft.

The propulsion system independent design variables include both continuous variables (e.g., thrust, wing area, fan pressure ratio) and discrete variables (e.g., overall pressure ratio, fan drive system, bypass nozzle architecture).

The aircraft synthesis and sizing analyses are carried out using NASA's Flight Optimization System (FLOPS) software, with enhancements to capture the impacts of large, ultra-high bypass ratio engines.
The detailed takeoff and landing trajectory calculations are used to establish the field length and certification noise levels for each aircraft-engine combination designed by the optimizer.
The exhaust emissions modeling focuses on oxides of nitrogen (NOx), which are produced through the thermal oxidation of nitrogen in the high-temperature regions of the engine combustor.
